meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'We Do Not Inherit the Earth from Our Ancestors; We Borrow It from Our Children'?
meta.ogDescription: Chief Seattle died in 1866. The saying's earliest close match is Wendell Berry, 1971 — and the chief's name was first attached to it in a 1991 US report.

answer.label: Not Chief Seattle — traced to Wendell Berry
answer.authorDates: 1934 – 2026 · Kentucky farmer, poet and environmental essayist
answer.sourceLine: Chief Seattle died in 1866, and this saying appears nowhere in his 1854 speech, in the supposed “letter to President Pierce,” or in any documented Native source. Quote Investigator ↗ finds the earliest close match in Wendell Berry’s 1971 book The Unforeseen Wilderness — “a man who knows that the world is not given by his fathers, but borrowed from his children” — and tentatively credits Berry with the first version of a maxim that then evolved, through many hands, into the polished wording sold on posters today.

source.excerpt: … a man who knows that the world is not given by his fathers, but borrowed from his children …
source.trailTitle: How a 1971 sentence became a chief’s
trail: 1971 — the earliest close match. Writing about Kentucky’s Red River Gorge as a dam threatened it, Wendell Berry praised “a man who knows that the world is not given by his fathers, but borrowed from his children.” Quote Investigator ↗ verified the line on paper at page 26 of The Unforeseen Wilderness and identifies it as the earliest close match; a scanned copy of the 1971 University Press of Kentucky edition ↗ is at the Internet Archive.

1974 — ‘given’ becomes ‘inherited’. On 13 November 1974, Australia’s environment minister Moses Henry Cass told an OECD meeting in Paris: “We have not inherited this earth from our parents to do with it what we will. We have borrowed it from our children.” QI ↗ notes that Cass swapped Berry’s “given” for “inherited” — the word every popular modern version now uses.

1991 — the chief’s name is attached. A report from the U.S. Council on Environmental Quality called the saying “timeless language” from “the Native American Chief Seattle,” giving no supporting citation — the credit QI records for the attribution. Chief Seattle had died in 1866, and the line is absent from the 1854 speech as Dr Henry A. Smith reconstructed it in the Seattle Sunday Star on 29 October 1887 ↗.

Even the ‘green’ Chief Seattle text is modern. The famous ecological speech that made him an environmental icon was written by screenwriter Ted Perry for the Southern Baptist Radio and Television Commission film Home, and the producer stripped Perry’s credit — see Wikipedia’s account ↗. Even that script does not contain this line: the University of Washington’s copy of Perry’s text ↗ has no borrowing-from-our-children sentence.
source.excerptNote: This is Berry’s phrasing, not the quotation as it circulates. Quote Investigator ↗ verified it on paper at page 26 and calls it the earliest close match; Berry reprinted the passage in Audubon magazine in May 1971, which carried it into conservation circles. The familiar “inherit…from our ancestors” wording is a later evolution by other hands.

source.rightsNote: The popular wording has no identifiable author, so no rights status can honestly be asserted for it. Its nearest documented ancestor — Wendell Berry’s sentence in The Unforeseen Wilderness, first published in 1971 — is well inside copyright and remains controlled by Berry’s estate and the University Press of Kentucky; quoting the short clause here is fair use for identification. Nothing about this saying is public domain by way of Chief Seattle, because nothing ties it to him.

author.name: Wendell Berry
author.kicker: The man who wrote the first version
author.heading: About Wendell Berry
author.metaLine: 1934 – 2026 · Kentucky farmer, poet, novelist and environmental essayist
author.bio: Wendell Erdman Berry (born 5 August 1934 in Louisville, Kentucky; died 31 August 2026 in Port Royal, Kentucky) farmed the same Henry County hillside he wrote about for more than half a century. He is best known for The Unsettling of America (1977) and The Gift of Good Land (1981), and for the Port William novels including Jayber Crow (2000) — a body of work built on the idea that land, community and economy are one subject, not three. His 1971 essay on Kentucky’s Red River Gorge, written as the valley faced being drowned by a dam, contains the sentence researchers now regard as this quotation’s starting point.

misattribution.heading: Everyone who has been given credit
misattribution.intro: Few sayings have collected as many owners. Quote Investigator ↗ documents the credit passing through at least eight named people and two anonymous folk traditions in roughly twenty years — and Chief Seattle arrives late in that sequence, not early.

items.why: The saying does not appear in his 1854 speech, in the letter he never wrote, or in any documented Native source. Professor Buzzkill ↗ concludes it “does not appear in either Chief Seattle’s ‘letter’ or his ‘speech’” and that there is no evidence he ever said it. Wikiquote’s Chief Seattle page ↗ does not carry the quotation at all.

In 1990 the U.S. Secretary of State introduced the maxim as Emerson’s: “Emerson, the 19th century American essayist and poet, put it this way…” Quotation expert Ralph Keyes, writing in the Washington Post in 1993, identified the speaker as James Baker and answered flatly: “Emerson didn’t say that.” ↗

A 1988 Los Angeles Times piece called it an “Amish saying”; a Celestial Seasonings tea box called it an “Amish belief.” Keyes dismissed both labels in 1993: “Neither is likely. The maxim is a little too perfectly tailored to today’s headlines.” ↗

items.who: David Brower, Lester Brown and Dennis J. Hall
items.why: Hall used the saying in quotation marks as an article title in July 1975 and was credited for it by 1976. The line was printed on the cover of Lester Brown’s Building a Sustainable Society, and Brown told David Brower he had got it from Brower — who replied that he did not remember ever saying it ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer is that this is a 1970s environmental maxim with no single author. Quote Investigator ↗ “would tentatively assign credit to Wendell Berry for crafting the first version of this statement which has been evolving for decades” — a careful, hedged conclusion, and the furthest any researcher has been able to push it.

context.heading: Why this one stuck to Chief Seattle
lead: Chief Seattle is a magnet for this kind of thing, and the reason is unusually well documented. The ecological speech that made him a global environmental symbol — the one about the earth being our mother and all things being connected — was not transcribed from him at all. It was written by a screenwriter, Ted Perry, for a documentary called Home made by the Southern Baptist Radio and Television Commission, and the producer removed Perry’s writing credit so the words would read as the chief’s own. Once a famous man has a famous speech he never gave, adding one more sentence to it costs nothing.

And the sentence fits so neatly. It is the argument of the entire environmental movement compressed into fifteen words, with a borrower and a lender and a debt. That is exactly what made Ralph Keyes suspicious in 1993: a maxim “a little too perfectly tailored to today’s headlines” is usually from today. The paper trail bears him out — it starts in a Kentucky river gorge in 1971, not on Puget Sound in 1854.
context.detailsSummary: The older precursor, and why it does not rescue the attribution
detailsBody: Quote Investigator does record something older, and it is worth stating plainly so nobody mistakes 1971 for the absolute beginning. The 1936 book Oscar Wilde Discovers America by Lloyd Lewis and Henry Justin Smith attributes to Wilde, during his 1882 visit to Canada, the remark: “The things of nature do not really belong to us, we should leave them to our children as we have received them.” That is a precursor thought, recorded half a century after the fact by biographers, not a version of this quotation.

Neither the Wilde precursor nor the Berry sentence points anywhere near Chief Seattle. The chain QI documents runs Berry (1971) → an Audubon Society attribution (1973) → Moses Henry Cass at the OECD (1974) → Dennis J. Hall in Michigan Natural Resources (1975) → UN and IUCN publications (1980–81) → Lester Brown and David Brower (1983–89) → Emerson (1990) → Chief Seattle (1991). The chief is the last name on the list, not the first.
context.pull: A chief who died in 1866 was first credited with this line in 1991, by a government report that gave no citation at all.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator identifies the earliest close match as Wendell Berry's 1971 book The Unforeseen Wilderness ('a man who knows that the world is not given by his fathers, but borrowed from his children'), verified on paper at page 26, chapter 2 'The One-Inch Journey', University Press of Kentucky, Lexington; reprinted in Audubon magazine, May 1971.

Quote Investigator records that on 13 November 1974 Australian Minister for the Environment Moses Henry Cass told an OECD meeting in Paris: 'We have not inherited this earth from our parents to do with it what we will. We have borrowed it from our children and we must be careful to use it in their interests as well as our own,' and notes Cass substituted 'inherited' for Berry's 'given'.

Quote Investigator records that in 1991 a report from the U.S. Council on Environmental Quality ascribed the saying to 'the Native American Chief Seattle', suggested the words were quite old, and gave no supporting citation.

Quote Investigator records the 1990 attribution to Ralph Waldo Emerson by the U.S. Secretary of State; Ralph Keyes in the Washington Post in 1993 named James Baker, wrote 'Emerson didn't say that', and dismissed both the 'Amish belief' and 'Native American proverb' labels as 'Neither is likely. The maxim is a little too perfectly tailored to today's headlines.'
Quote Investigator's conclusion: 'QI would tentatively assign credit to Wendell Berry for crafting the first version of this statement which has been evolving for decades.'

Quote Investigator records a precursor attributed to Oscar Wilde in the 1936 book 'Oscar Wilde Discovers America' by Lloyd Lewis and Henry Justin Smith (page 350), regarding Wilde's 1882 Canadian visit: 'The things of nature do not really belong to us, we should leave them to our children as we have received them.'

Quote Investigator records Dennis J. Hall's July 1975 article in Michigan Natural Resources, the 1988 Los Angeles Times 'Amish saying' label, the cover of Lester Brown's Building a Sustainable Society, and David Brower saying he did not remember having said it.

Professor Buzzkill concludes the quotation 'does not appear in either Chief Seattle's letter or his speech', that there is no evidence he ever said it, and identifies Wendell Berry's 1971 Unforeseen Wilderness as the nearest originator Buzzkill Institute researchers could find.

Wikiquote's Chief Seattle page has sections 'Quotes', the 1855 statement on surrendering tribal lands, 'Misattributed', 'Quotes about Chief Seattle' and 'External links'; this quotation does not appear anywhere on the page. The page states widely circulated quotes were 'shown in 1992 to have been a fiction, devised by television scriptwriter Ted Perry'.

Wikipedia records that Chief Seattle was a leader of the Duwamish and Suquamish peoples who died on 7 June 1866; that he delivered a speech in 1854 reported by Dr Henry A. Smith in the Seattle Sunday Star in 1887; and that the accuracy of Smith's account is doubtful.

Wikipedia records that Smith's version was published in the Seattle Sunday Star on 29 October 1887, that William Arrowsmith made a modified version in the late 1960s, that Ted Perry wrote an adaptation for a film called Home produced by the Southern Baptist Radio and Television Commission, and that the producer removed Perry's writing credit and attributed the text directly to Chief Seattle. The article does not report this quotation appearing in any version of the speech.

The University of Washington's classroom page reproduces Ted Perry's text, credited as a 'film script for Home' produced by the Southern Baptist Radio and Television Commission; the borrowing-from-our-children formulation does not appear in Perry's text as presented there.

The Internet Archive catalog record lists 'The unforeseen wilderness: an essay on Kentucky's Red River Gorge' by Berry, Wendell, 1934-, published Lexington: The University Press of Kentucky, 1971, with 'The one-inch journey' in the table of contents.

Wikipedia records Wendell Erdman Berry's dates as 5 August 1934 (Louisville, Kentucky) to 31 August 2026 (Port Royal, Kentucky), describes him as an American novelist, poet, essayist, environmental activist and farmer, and lists The Unforeseen Wilderness (1971, University Press of Kentucky, photographs by Ralph Eugene Meatyard) among his works.
